lesson.menu_desc: The Meridian case study told live on a client panel -- inversion after negative adverbials (Never had we lost a client that fast; Not only did we publish the numbers; Only after the report started did adoption climb) -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 19 -- Telling the Story on Stage -- The Client Panel
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Izabel Cristina de Pieri | Lesson 19 -- Telling the Story on Stage

listenings.text: Izabel, it is David Chen. I am at the airport, boarding in twenty minutes, so listen rather than call back. I have been thinking about how we split this on stage. You take the failure. I take the recovery. That order matters, because if I open with how good the fix was, nobody in that room believes me, and rightly so. Here is what I am going to say when the moderator turns to me. I am going to say that at no point did AVRT ask us to keep the failure quiet, and that never in eleven years of buying components had I seen a supplier publish a number that made it look worse. That is the whole reason I agreed to sit next to you. One warning, though. There is a purchasing director from Ohio in the front row who will ask you what it cost. Do not dodge it. Give her the eleven months and let her do the math herself. And Izabel, please do not read from your notes. Rehearse it tonight, then leave the paper in the hotel room.

Good morning, Izabel. Sofia here with the run of show for tomorrow. Your panel is at eleven fifteen, right after the keynote, in the main hall. Forty minutes total: twenty-five with the moderator, fifteen for questions from the floor. The moderator is Marcus Hale, and he sent me his three questions in advance, which is unusual and very helpful. One, how bad was it. Two, why publish the numbers instead of the apology. Three, what you would tell a room full of suppliers who are afraid of the same thing. Two practical notes from the production team. There is no lectern, so you will be on a stool with a handheld microphone, which means no notes and no slides. And they record everything, so whatever you say becomes a clip. My advice is to decide your one line before you walk on, the line you would be happy to see quoted out of context, because that is exactly what will happen. I have booked the room at nine tonight if you want to rehearse it out loud with me.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a short true story you tell to make a bigger point
the person who runs a public discussion and asks the questions
the quality that makes an audience believe what you say
the nervousness you feel just before speaking in public
a small group of invited speakers who discuss a topic in front of an audience
said with no preparation and no notes
the opening line that makes an audience want to keep listening
a short memorable phrase that people quote afterwards
